title: Range Proofs — From Naive to Bulletproofs

questions.question: What is the typical form of a Pedersen commitment to a value v with blinding r (multiplicative notation)?
options: C = g^v · h^r (mod p), for generators g and h.
C = H(v || r), where H is a cryptographic hash function.
C = v·g + r·h (mod p), where g and h are integers.
C = g^(v+r) (mod p), using a single generator.
questions.explanation: A Pedersen commitment combines the value exponent under g and a random blinding exponent under h.

questions.question: If v is represented in binary as v = Σ 2^i·b_i, what constraint must each b_i satisfy for a range check?
options: Each b_i must be either 0 or 1.
Each b_i must be uniformly random in Z_q.
Each b_i must be an odd integer.
Each b_i must be a generator of the group.
questions.explanation: A binary decomposition is only meaningful for a range check when every digit is constrained to {0,1}.

questions.question: Why do systems with Pedersen commitments typically require a range proof for hidden amounts?
options: Because without it, values wrap modulo q and a prover can commit to negative/overflow values while still passing algebraic checks.
Because commitments reveal v unless you add a range proof.
Because a range proof makes commitments perfectly binding instead of computationally binding.
Because a range proof is needed to compute modular inverses.
questions.explanation: Commitments alone only enforce equations modulo the group order; a range proof constrains the real-world interpretation.

questions.question: In the lesson’s bit proof, the prover OR-proves one of two Schnorr statements under base h. What are those statements for a bit commitment C = g^b · h^r?
options: Either C = h^r (b=0) or C/g = h^r (b=1).
Either C = g^r (b=0) or C/h = g^r (b=1).
Either C = g^b (b=0) or C = h^b (b=1).
Either C = g^(b+r) or C = h^(b+r).
questions.explanation: Dividing by g removes the b=1 factor, reducing both cases to a discrete-log statement under h.

questions.question: What does the recomposed commitment D = Π C_i^{2^i} represent if each C_i commits to bit b_i with blinding r_i?
options: A commitment to v = Σ 2^i·b_i with combined blinding r' = Σ 2^i·r_i.
A commitment to Σ b_i with combined blinding Σ r_i.
A commitment to the product Π b_i with combined blinding Π r_i.
A commitment to a random value independent of the bits.
questions.explanation: Exponentiating by 2^i and multiplying uses the homomorphism: exponents add, so bits and blindings combine linearly.

questions.question: Why does the lesson require choosing n such that 2^n < q?
options: So the value range doesn’t wrap around modulo q, making the statement “v is in [0, 2^n)” unambiguous.
So the verifier doesn’t need to check any proofs for the bits.
So the group modulus p can be smaller than the value range.
So the OR proof can omit the c1 + c2 = c check.
questions.explanation: If 2^n reaches q, different integers become the same element modulo q and the range statement loses meaning.

questions.question: In Fiat–Shamir-style proofs, what should the challenge hash bind to prevent replay/transplant attacks?
options: A domain label plus all statement inputs and commitments in the transcript.
Only the last commitment value, to keep hashing fast.
Only the prover’s responses, because they contain the witness.
Only the group modulus p, because everything else is derived.
questions.explanation: If you don’t hash the full statement and transcript, a proof can be reused in a different context or for a different statement.

questions.question: In the demo, why does verification fail when the verifier uses a different label than the prover used?
options: Because the label changes the Fiat–Shamir challenges, so the proof no longer matches the verifier’s recomputed challenges.
Because the label changes the group generator g.
Because the label changes the committed value v.
Because the label disables subgroup checks.
questions.explanation: The label is part of domain separation; changing it changes the challenge and invalidates the transcript.
